GUI

GUI builds native desktop interfaces from composable windows, controls, dialogs, themes, actions, password-safe input, and Pixel drawing.

An Gui.Application owns surfaces and drives the event loop. Each Gui.Surface has a root Gui.Wnd; controls form a flatly documented API and are connected at runtime through parent links, event hooks, signals, docking, and layout constraints.

Create a window

using Core, Gui var app: Application #main { let surface = (try app.createSurface( 100, 100, 640, 420, SurfaceFlags.StandardWindow))! surface.setTitle("My application") let button = PushButton.create(surface.view(), "Continue") button.dockStyle = .CenterKeepSizeVert surface.show() return app.run() }

Coordinates and sizes are logical pixels. Windows are owned by their application; use Gui.Wnd.destroy for deferred destruction during event dispatch.

Finite transitions use the application-owned Gui.Animator. Typed tracks can be retargeted by Gui.AnimationChannel, grouped in parallel or sequence, and are cancelled automatically when their target is hidden or destroyed. See help/08-animation.md for the motion and presentation contract.

Application and surfaces

Gui.Application owns the renderer, theme, input state, surfaces, timers, and event queue. A typical program creates one application value, creates its main Gui.Surface, populates the surface's root view, then enters Gui.Application.run.

using Core, Gui var app: Application #main { let surface = (try app.createSurface( 100, 100, 640, 420, SurfaceFlags.StandardWindow))! surface.setTitle("Tasks") let view = surface.view() PushButton.create(view, "Add task") surface.show() return app.run() }

The first surface initializes the selected Pixel.IRenderer and default theme. OpenGL is selected by default. To use the CPU renderer or a third-party backend, select it before creating the first surface; the concrete renderer must outlive the application:

var cpu: Pixel.RenderCpu var app: Application app.setRenderer(&cpu) let surface = (try app.createSurface(0, 0, 640, 420))!

Additional surfaces use the same renderer and participate in the same event loop. Their painters are bound automatically; paint handlers use the renderer exposed by Gui.PaintContext.

Use Gui.Application.postEvent to enqueue work for the UI loop. Gui.Application.sendEvent dispatches immediately and should only be used when the caller is already on the UI thread and understands event propagation.

Windows and layout

Gui.Wnd is the common base of controls. A window belongs to a Gui.Surface, can own child windows, and stores its position in its parent's local coordinate system.

Create concrete controls with their create function. The generic Gui.Wnd.create helper is useful when defining a custom control.

Choose a layout mechanism

NeedAPI
Attach a child to one edgeGui.DockStyle
Preserve distances while the parent resizesGui.AnchorStyle
Express content, fill, and expansion preferencesGui.LayoutSpec
Place rows, columns, stacks, or split regionsLayout controls
Perform one-off absolute placementGui.Wnd.setPosition

Margins occupy space outside a control; padding reduces its client content area. Call Gui.Wnd.invalidateLayout after changing a value that affects measurement. The framework then measures and arranges the affected tree.

Let the content decide

An axis you leave unsized belongs to the content. Gui.Wnd.measure asks the window through Gui.IWnd.measureContent, and the answer becomes its preferred size: a caption widens its button, a list of entries widens its combo box, a wrapped paragraph reports the height it needs at the width it is offered, and a band docked with no height is as tall as what it holds. An axis carrying a size the caller stated keeps it, unmeasured.

// The height is a design decision; the width is the caption's business. let action = PushButton.create(bar, "Create encrypted vault", {0, 0, 0, 36})

This is what keeps a surface correct when its text changes — a translation, a document title, a user-supplied name. Implement measureContent on a custom control that draws its own text or items; the default reports nothing, which keeps the authored size on both axes.

Use coordinate conversion methods on Gui.Wnd when crossing local, surface, and screen spaces. Keep hit testing and painting in the coordinate system named by the event or drawing API.

Events, actions, and lifetime

GUI events implement Gui.IEvent and travel through a target window and its owners. A control can implement the typed handlers from Gui.IWnd, or install a Gui.HookEvent for lightweight interception.

Common event families include:

EventPurpose
Gui.CreateEvent and Gui.DestroyEventLifetime transitions
Gui.ResizeEventGeometry changes
Gui.PaintEventDrawing passes
Gui.KeyEvent and Gui.MouseEventUser input
Gui.CommandEventSemantic commands
Gui.TimerEvent and Gui.FrameEventScheduled and per-frame work
Gui.NotifyEventControl-specific notifications

Events are synchronous unless posted with Gui.Application.postEvent or Gui.Wnd.postEvent. A handler can mark an event unaccepted so it continues to an owner.

Actions and command IDs decouple menus, buttons, and shortcuts from the code that performs an operation. Compute command state in one place so every presentation receives the same enabled, checked, name, and icon state.

Reaching every control from the keyboard

A key goes to the focused window, then to its owners, and what none of them accepts becomes navigation: a shortcut registered on the chain first, then Tab and Shift+Tab through the traversal stops of the surface, then Enter and Escape for Gui.Surface.defaultButton and Gui.Surface.cancelButton. A control that wants one of those keys for itself only has to accept the event — that is how the rich editor keeps its tabulation and the property grid keeps its row-to-row Tab.

Two declarations put a control in that order:

  • Gui.Wnd.focusPolicy says whether a pointer press focuses the window and whether the traversal stops on it. A plain container declares nothing and is walked through.
  • Gui.Wnd.focusDelegate points at the inner window that reads the keys, so a composite is one stop however many windows it is built from. Its parts declare Gui.FocusPolicy.Inner and disappear from the order.

The order itself is Gui.FocusOrder: depth first, and between siblings the order their rectangles read, because a container does not place its children in the order it created them. Nothing has to be numbered, and nothing has to be renumbered when a control is inserted.

Call Gui.Wnd.setInitialFocus once a surface is built so it opens ready for the keyboard; Gui.Wnd.hasVisibleFocus is true only while the keyboard is what moved the focus, and Gui.Wnd.showsFocusRing is what a widget paints its focus ring from: it adds the diagnostic that draws every ring of a surface at once.

Call Gui.Wnd.destroy from handlers. Destruction is deferred until dispatch is safe; do not retain control pointers after their destroy event.

Taking a drop from the desktop

Every surface is a drop target from the moment it is created, so a window takes drags from Explorer and from other applications without asking for anything. A gesture carrying a payload is delivered as a Gui.DragDropEvent to the window under the pointer, and it bubbles to the ancestors exactly like a mouse event: a control that ignores drops costs nothing, and a container can answer for the whole of its content.

Four phases bracket one gesture. Enter and Leave say when the pointer is over the window, which is what a drop highlight is turned on and off by — Leave is delivered when the drag is cancelled or dropped elsewhere too, so a highlight is never stuck on. Over repeats while the pointer moves inside the window, and Drop is the release.

A target claims the gesture by setting Gui.DragDropEvent.effect to one member of Gui.DragDropEvent.allowed; leaving it at None rejects the drop and lets the event bubble further. Gui.pickDropEffect answers the desktop convention — Control copies, Shift moves, both together link — restricted to what the source permits, so a target that has no policy of its own is one line:

mtd impl onDragDropEvent(evt: *DragDropEvent) { let path = evt.data.singleFile() if !path or !Path.hasExtension(path!, ".scrypt") { evt.accepted = false return } if evt.kind == .Drop do .openContainer(path) evt.effect = pickDropEffect(evt.allowed & (DropEffect.Copy | DropEffect.Link), evt.modifiers) }

Gui.DragData is the payload, borrowed for the duration of one callback: a target that wants to keep a path, a text or an image copies it out. It answers safely whatever the drag carries — Gui.DragData.hasFiles, Gui.DragData.singleFile, Gui.DragData.hasText and Gui.DragData.hasImage are all cheap, and only Gui.DragData.image pays for a decode. That matters because a drag hovering a window asks the same questions on every mouse move.

Two controls already answer for themselves. An Gui.EditBox takes dropped text at the character under the pointer, and with Gui.EditBoxFlags.AcceptFileDrop a single dropped file replaces its content with that path — which is what a field naming a document wants, and what Properties.FilePath declares on a property-grid row.

A test drives the whole path with no desktop under it: Testing.HeadlessHost.dropFilesOnWnd releases a payload on one control, Testing.HeadlessHost.dragFilesOver moves a gesture across the tree, and Testing.HeadlessHost.cancelDrag ends one the way Escape does.

Dragging out of a window

Gui.Wnd.startDrag carries a payload to whatever the pointer is released on, and answers with the single effect the target settled on. The same Gui.DragData is what a source fills: Gui.DragData.addFile, Gui.DragData.setText and Gui.DragData.setImage say what is on offer, and offering several is the useful case rather than a redundant one — a folder takes the file, a picture editor takes the bitmap, and each target picks what it understands.

var data: DragData data.addFile(exportedPath) try data.setImage(picture) discard thumbnail.startDrag(&data, DropEffect.Copy)

A press only becomes a drag once the pointer has travelled far enough, which Gui.Wnd.exceedsDragThreshold answers from the distance the desktop is configured with, so a shaky hand on a click does not start dragging.

Two consequences of the desktop running the gesture are worth knowing before writing the handler. The call does not return until the drop, and the window stops painting for that whole time — every application that drags behaves this way. And the button that started the drag comes back up inside that loop, so the control has to forget its own press before calling, rather than waiting for a release event that will never arrive:

if evt.kind == .Move and .pressedItem != Swag.U64.Max { if .exceedsDragThreshold(.pressOrigin, evt.surfacePos) { .pressedItem = Swag.U64.Max // no release event follows the gesture .dragOutItem() return } }

Painting and themes

Paint handlers receive a Gui.PaintEvent whose Gui.PaintContext connects the current Pixel painter and renderer. Drawing uses the same logical-pixel coordinate system as the window. Gui.Application.renderer is a Pixel.IRenderer, so the same paint path can target OpenGL in a native application, Pixel.RenderCpu in deterministic tests, or another renderer selected through Gui.Application.setRenderer.

The theme is separated into:

PartRole
Gui.ThemePaletteThe thirty-odd decisions a theme makes
Gui.ThemeColorsSemantic colors for controls and states, all derived from the palette
Gui.ThemeMetricsSizes, spacing, borders, and timing
Gui.ThemeImageRectsRegions and painted corner radii in the theme image atlas
Gui.ThemeStyleA control's resolved font, colors, and resources

A palette is where a theme is written: grounds, rules, ink, one accent and the ink drawn on it, status hues, a veil, and the chrome of a window. Gui.ThemeColors.apply turns those into a value for every painted part, which is what makes a theme complete by construction — it cannot answer for a button and forget the field beside it. The four shipped palettes (Gui.Theme.setDark, Gui.Theme.setLight, Gui.Theme.setSwagDark, Gui.Theme.setSwagLight) are token lists and nothing else, and each also restores the geometry it implies.

The Swag palettes use one small four-logical-pixel corner for bounded interface parts: fields, actions, rectangular tool cells, hover and selection grounds, and standalone raised panels. Joined bars, rails, separators, and document grounds remain square; the outer surface uses its larger Gui.ThemeMetrics.surfaceWnd_CornerRadius. Set a window's Gui.Wnd.backgroundStyle to Gui.BackgroundStyle.Panel when it is a raised panel rather than joined application chrome, so its ground follows that geometry in every palette.

var palette = Gui.ThemeColors.swagDarkPalette() palette.accent = 0xFF00A0FF palette.onAccent = 0xFF000000 app.theme.setPalette(palette) app.notifyThemeChanged()

bin/examples/modules/gui10 is the theme inspector: it lists every color of every palette by reflection, flags any value one palette answers for and another does not, and shows every widget in every state.

Read theme data through the current window so custom controls respect local style overrides:

let colors = wnd.getThemeColors() let metrics = wnd.getThemeMetrics() let font = wnd.getFont()

Paint only inside the invalidated region when possible. Call Gui.Wnd.invalidate after a visual state change, and Gui.Wnd.invalidateRect when only a bounded region changed. Gui.Application.notifyThemeChanged recomputes styles and invalidates the interface after editing shared theme data.

Headless paint tests

Gui.Testing.HeadlessHost builds a deterministic application and widget tree without creating an OS window. Gui.Testing.HeadlessHost.render runs the normal surface paint pipeline through Pixel's software renderer and returns owned pixels.

#test { var host: Testing.HeadlessHost host.setup(160, 80) discard PushButton.create(&host.root, "Continue", {20, 20, 120, 32}) let image = host.render() Pixel.Testing.assertImageGolden(&image, "continue-button") }

Use structural and event assertions for behavior, command goldens for emitted paint operations, and PNG goldens for the final composition. A small OpenGL integration suite remains necessary for context, shader compiler, and driver coverage.

Controls and dialogs

GUI supplies primitive controls, composite controls, and modal dialogs. Start with the narrowest control that represents the user's intent:

NeedControl
Trigger a commandGui.PushButton or Gui.Button
Display text or an iconGui.Label
Edit a short valueGui.EditBox
Edit structured textGui.RichEditCtrl
Present rows or hierarchyGui.ListCtrl or tree controls
Scroll arbitrary contentGui.ScrollWnd
Present commandsGui.MenuCtrl
Edit reflected propertiesGui.PropertiesCtrl

Controls expose signals for local reactions and command IDs for application-wide actions. Prefer command IDs when the same operation appears in menus, toolbars, shortcuts, and context menus.

Dialogs own a temporary surface and run a modal loop while keeping the application responsive. Gui.MessageDlg, Gui.FileDlg, and Gui.EditDlg cover common interactions; derive from Gui.Dialog when a workflow needs a custom arrangement or validation.

Rich text and properties

Gui.RichEditCtrl provides multi-line editing, selections, undoable commands, lexical styling, and viewport management. Its cursor and selection values use text positions defined by the rich-edit model rather than Pixel coordinates.

Keep model operations separate from painting:

  1. Apply text or selection commands.
  2. Let the control update layout and undo state.
  3. Invalidate the affected view.
  4. Respond to semantic notifications outside the editor.

The property system builds editors from reflected values and metadata. Gui.Properties describes a property source, Gui.PropertiesItem represents one row, and Gui.PropertiesCtrl presents the editable tree. Attributes such as category, display name, and description keep domain-specific labels beside the data model.

Use the provided undo layer when edits must be reversible. Validation belongs at the model boundary: the editor can report invalid input without committing a partially converted value.

Markdown documents

Gui.Markdown.View is the reusable, read-only Markdown document widget. Use Gui.Markdown.View.createText for an in-memory document and Gui.Markdown.View.createFile to stream UTF-8 source without blocking the application on the whole file. Both forms use Gui.Markdown.Style for reading measure, insets, and type sizes; Gui.Markdown.Style.theme is the standard theme-following style.

let markdown = Markdown.View.createFile(parent, fileName, Markdown.Style.theme()) markdown.sigLinkActivated += func(view, url) { discard view Env.openUrl(url) }

The renderer supports GFM headings, lists, tasks, fenced code, tables, autolinks, reference links, alerts, footnotes, metadata, and thematic rules, plus Typora-style highlight, subscript, superscript, table of contents, and TeX delimiters. Inline and display TeX are laid out by Pixel.MathExpression; the widget does not substitute approximate Unicode glyphs or execute embedded HTML.

Every surface, rule, link, selection, notice, and text color comes from the active GUI theme. A theme change relayouts the document and all mathematical expressions without rebuilding the source model.

Resources and localization

Every Gui.Application owns a Core.Resources.Bundle in Gui.Application.resources. A resource is a run of bytes addressed by a /-separated name, such as theme/widgets.png or lang/fr/gui.tweak. The embedded content of every loaded module registers itself as the fallback provider, so a bare application needs no configuration; a disk folder added before the first surface lets files override any of those names without recompiling:

var app: Application #main { // Files under datas/ now override the embedded theme art, fonts, // theme sheets, and language files of the same name. app.resources.addFolder("datas") let surface = notnull (try app.createSurface(100, 100, 640, 420, SurfaceFlags.StandardWindow)) surface.show() return app.run() }

Theme sheets

A theme sheet is a tweak text with up to four folders whose keys are the reflected field names of Gui.ThemePalette, Gui.ThemeColors, Gui.ThemeMetrics, and Gui.ThemeImageRects. An omitted key keeps its current value, so a sheet is a delta over the active theme, and $name copies another key of the same folder:

/ThemePalette ground 0xFF161310 text 0xFFEDE4D4 accent 0xFFD79921 /ThemeColors btnPush_Bk 0xFF202026 /ThemeMetrics btnPush_Height 32 /ThemeImageRects btnPush_Normal {{1 29 27 27} 0} btnPush_Hot $btnPush_Normal

A whole theme is the first folder and nothing else: naming any palette token re-derives every semantic color from the tokens, so a sheet of thirty lines answers for the three hundred parts of the interface and cannot leave one of them carrying the color of the theme it started from. The other folders are for the parts a theme wants different from what its own tokens derive, and they are read after the derivation whatever order they appear in. bin/examples/modules/gui10/src/sepia.tweak is a complete worked sheet.

Apply a sheet with Gui.Theme.applySheet, or resolve themes/<name>.tweak through the bundle and refresh every surface with Gui.Application.loadTheme. An unknown key fails with the faulty line number, so a broken sheet is reported instead of half-applied silently.

String tables

Visible strings live in structs of string fields whose declared values are the reference English wording. The GUI module owns Gui.Strings, read through Gui.strings; an application declares its own table the same way and registers it once with Gui.registerStrings:

struct AppStrings { mainTitle: string = "My application" } var g_AppStrings: AppStrings #main { Gui.registerStrings'AppStrings(&g_AppStrings, "myapp") // ... }

A language file is one key value line per overridden field, resolved as the resource lang/<tag>/<file>.tweak. A key the file omits keeps its reference value, so a translation only carries what it changes. Gui.Application.setLanguage retargets every registered table and sends a LanguageChanged notification through every surface; command-driven controls pick the new wording up on their next update, while text set once at construction must listen for the notification or be rebuilt.

Languages

A tag is only presentable once it is registered with its name, so a picker can list what the application ships without hard-coding it:

Gui.registerLanguage("fr", "FranÃ§ais")

Gui.ReferenceLanguage — "en" — is always registered and always comes first: it names the declared reference wording and needs no resource file. Gui.languages returns what a picker should show, and a language is named in its own words, so those names are never translated.

English is the language an application starts in. Following the account instead is a choice the user makes, not a guess the application makes on its behalf: Gui.systemLanguage resolves Core.Env.userLocaleName against the registered tags and falls back to the reference language, and Gui.Application.setSystemLanguage applies it. Applying a tag that was never registered fails rather than silently presenting itself as applied.

Embed the translation and validate it when the module compiles: a mistyped key becomes a build error with its line number instead of a runtime fallback.

const FrenchStrings = #include("lang/fr/myapp.tweak") #run { expect Gui.validateStrings'AppStrings(cast(string) FrenchStrings) }

Wording a literal cannot carry

Two places state a wording where a string table cannot reach: a property attribute and a menu item built from a literal. Both have a hook.

A property attribute value is a compile-time constant, so the grid generates #[Properties.Name("Thickness")] exactly as declared. Install one resolver and that literal becomes a key instead — every label, description, category segment, heading, note, unit and enumeration entry the grid builds passes through it:

Properties.setTextResolver(func(key: string)->#null string { switch key { case "Thickness": return appStrings().propThickness } return null })

Answer null for a string the resolver does not own: the strings this module declares answer next, and the declared wording stands when nobody does. Rows resolve as they are built, so rebuild a grid that has to follow a switch — Gui.PropertiesCtrl.clear and the same addStruct calls again.

A menu bar copies the wording into its item once, so the entries of a bar built at start-up would keep the language they were built in while everything below them refreshes through the command state. Build them from a Gui.MenuLabelResolver instead, and the label is read again on every layout:

topMenu.addPopup(func()->string => appStrings().menuFile, fileMenu)

Sizes belong to the text

Translated wording is longer than the reference more often than not, so a surface that survives a language switch is one that never wrote its sizes down. Leave an axis unsized and the layout pass asks the window itself through Gui.IWnd.measureContent: a button widens with its caption, a combo box with its widest entry, a wrapped paragraph grows taller, and a band docked without a height is as tall as what it holds. An axis carrying an explicit size keeps it, so this is opt-in per widget and per axis.

// Width measured from the caption, height stated because the row is a design decision. let action = PushButton.create(card, appStrings().createVault, {0, 0, 0, 36}) // A paragraph that decides its own height, whatever the language costs. let help = Label.create(card, appStrings().createHelp, {}, null, .WordWrap | .SecondaryText | .AutoHeight) help.dockStyle = .Top

Re-label with Gui.Button.setText, Gui.Label.setText and Gui.FormLayoutCtrl.setRowLabel when the notification arrives, then arrange again: the sizes follow the new wording on their own. Prove it rather than trust it — Gui.Testing.assertContentFits walks a surface and fails on the first window smaller than what it says it needs, so a test that loops over Gui.languages is enough to keep every shipped translation honest.

Animation

Every Gui.Application owns one Gui.Animator. It advances finite tracks from the application frame clock, updates only their target windows, and releases each callback when the track completes or is cancelled. A window being hidden or destroyed cancels every track that targets it.

Use a stable Gui.AnimationChannel for one logical property. Starting another track with the same target and channel replaces the previous one and begins at the value currently on screen. This makes repeated pointer input, resizing, and live theme changes retarget without a jump.

Animate a typed value

The scheduler supports f32, Pixel.Color, Math.Point, Math.Vector4, and Math.Rectangle. The update callback says exactly which state changes; the track's Gui.AnimationImpact says whether that state needs paint or layout.

var options: AnimationOptions options.duration = 180'ms options.easing = .EaseOut discard app.animator.animatePoint( panel, AnimationChannel.from("Example.PanelOffset"), {-24, 0}, {}, func(wnd, value) { wnd.setPresentationOffset(value); }, options)

An Gui.AnimationHandle does not retain the target. Keep it only when an operation needs to cancel or inspect that exact run. Prefer stable, descriptive channel names over global counters: the channel is what gives retargeting its property identity.

Coordinate tracks

An Gui.AnimationGroup starts tracks together or in insertion order. Transfer the completed group to the scheduler with #move.

var group = AnimationGroup.parallel() group.addF32(card, AnimationChannel.from("Example.CardOpacity"), 0, 1, func(wnd, value) { wnd.setPresentationOpacity(value); }, options) group.addPoint(card, AnimationChannel.from("Example.CardOffset"), {16, 0}, {}, func(wnd, value) { wnd.setPresentationOffset(value); }, options) discard app.animator.start(#move group)

Use Gui.AnimationGroup.sequence for a short ordered disclosure. Springs, keyframes, and reflection-based field mutation are deliberately outside this API: each track remains bounded, typed, and explicit about its invalidation cost.

Choose a curve

Gui.AnimationEasing carries nine shapes. The first four stay inside the zero-to-one interval and suit any value, including opacity and color. The five others anticipate or overshoot on purpose, which reads as weight on a position or a scale and as nothing at all on a value the compositor clamps:

  • EaseInBack, EaseOutBack and EaseInOutBack pull back before leaving and pass their endpoint before settling on it.
  • EaseOutElastic springs well past the endpoint and oscillates onto it.
  • EaseOutBounce lands and rebounds, each rebound shorter than the last.

Core.Math.CurvePreset.evaluate answers the same function the scheduler applies, so a preview plots exactly what a track will do.

Repeat a track

Gui.AnimationOptions.repeatCount plays a track several times in a row, and zero repeats it until something cancels it. Gui.AnimationOptions.autoReverse runs every second play backwards, which turns a pair of plays into a ping-pong that ends where it started.

var options: AnimationOptions options.duration = 900'ms options.easing = .EaseInOut options.repeatCount = 0 options.autoReverse = true options.motion = .Essential discard app.animator.animateF32(dot, AnimationChannel.from("Example.Pulse"), 1, 0.4, func(wnd, value) { wnd.setPresentationOpacity(value); }, options)

An endless track never gives its turn back, so keep one in a parallel group rather than in the middle of a sequence. Reduced motion collapses an endless decorative loop to the state it keeps returning to instead of leaving it running behind a preference that asked for none.

Keep geometry logical

Gui.Wnd.presentationOpacity, Gui.Wnd.presentationOffset, Gui.Wnd.presentationScale, and Gui.Wnd.presentationClip affect painting for the complete window subtree. They do not change layout, hit testing, or keyboard focus. This is the normal choice for decorative movement; call Gui.Wnd.resetPresentation from completion when a custom transition has finished, so a settled window costs the painter nothing.

A scale turns around Gui.Wnd.presentationPivot, normalized inside the logical rectangle, and Gui.Wnd.presentationRect reports where the window is actually seen. A scaled or faded subtree composites through one off-screen layer, so a factor far above one softens text: scale is for arrival, emphasis, and press feedback, not for zooming a view.

For a size that must participate in layout, use an .Layout track or Gui.Animator.animateLayoutHeight. Layout animation is intentionally separate because it can remeasure and arrange a larger tree on every frame.

Gui.Animator.transitionPage implements the standard restrained page arrival. Logical visibility moves to the incoming page immediately, while the outgoing page fades out beneath it until the handoff completes; the page area therefore never passes through an empty frame. A Gui.Tab can opt into it with Gui.Tab.setPageTransitions. gui11 is the executable example for the curve gallery, staggered groups, retargeting under interruption, endless loops, layout animation, and reduced motion.

Respect reduced motion

Gui.MotionPreference.System follows the Windows client-area-animation setting and refreshes when platform settings change. Applications and tests can override it with Gui.Application.setMotionPreference. Decorative tracks complete immediately under reduced motion; .Essential tracks keep running for feedback such as indeterminate progress, without requiring large translation or scale.

Durations and travel distances come from the motion fields in Gui.ThemeMetrics, so a theme can tune quick feedback, page changes, and layout-affecting panels as one system.

Test exact progress

Gui.Testing.HeadlessHost defaults to reduced motion so existing widget snapshots remain at their resting pixels. A motion test enables full motion with Gui.Testing.HeadlessHost.setReducedMotion, samples exact intervals with Gui.Testing.HeadlessHost.advanceAnimations, and can complete all remaining tracks with Gui.Testing.HeadlessHost.finishAnimations.

type alias Gui.AnimationEasing #src

Selects the interpolation curve applied to normalized animation progress.

The toolkit does not own its curves: a named easing is one shape of Core.Math.Curve, and the scheduler evaluates it through that type like any curve an application authors itself. Set Gui.AnimationOptions.curve instead to drive a track with a shape that has no name here.

The last five curves leave the zero-to-one interval on purpose: an anticipating or overshooting track passes beyond its endpoints before settling on them. Use them for position, scale, and other geometry that can travel past its target, and keep the first four for opacity and color, where an out-of-range value is clamped rather than seen.

alias AnimationEasing = Math.CurvePreset

Field details

curve#

Authored curve applied to normalized progress instead of easing.

The scheduler borrows it rather than copying it, so it has to outlive every track it was given to — a curve owned by the animated window, by its theme, or by the application all qualify, and a temporary declared next to the call does not. Leave it null to use easing.

Field details

focusVisible#

Whether the keyboard focus must be shown.

Keyboard traversal turns it on and a pointer press turns it off, so a control acted on with the mouse keeps the focus without a ring around it while a surface being driven from the keyboard always says where the keyboard is. Widgets read it through Gui.Wnd.hasVisibleFocus.

maxRunFrame#

Stops the run loop after this many frames, or never when zero. A test or a scripted run sets it to bound the loop without a user closing the window.

resources#

Named resources of the application: theme art, fonts, theme sheets, and language files. The embedded content of every loaded module registers itself as the fallback, so a bare application needs no configuration; add a disk folder before creating the first surface to let files override any of those names.

surfaces#

The surface list is maintained by the application: create and destroy surfaces through its own API so the modal stack and the render loop stay consistent.

struct Gui.DragContent #src

One file a payload carries by content instead of by a path on disk.

A mail attachment is the shape this exists for: it has a name and it has bytes, and no file on any disk holds it. A source offers one so a picture reaches a folder or a message without being written to the temporary folder first, and a target reads one so an attachment dragged out of a client arrives with its content rather than as nothing at all.

The bytes are produced when a target finally asks for them. A gesture announces what it carries long before anything is dropped, and most gestures end over something that never asks.

struct Gui.DragData #src

Payload of one drag gesture, in both directions.

A target reads it: the value belongs to the framework and is borrowed for the duration of one Gui.DragDropEvent callback and no longer, so a window that wants to keep a path, a text or an image copies it out. Every accessor is safe on a drag that carries nothing of that kind.

A source fills it: Gui.DragData.addFile, Gui.DragData.addContent, Gui.DragData.setText and Gui.DragData.setImage say what the gesture offers, and Gui.Wnd.startDrag carries it to whatever the pointer is released on. Offering both a file and an image is the useful case rather than a redundant one — a folder takes the file, a picture editor takes the bitmap.

Nothing is produced before a target asks for it, because a drag hovering a window announces its formats long before anything is dropped. Gui.DragData.hasImage answers without decoding or encoding anything and Gui.DragData.image is what pays for the decode; a content file is the same rule spelled out in Gui.DragContent.

struct Gui.DragDropEvent #src

Carries one phase of a drag and drop gesture over a window.

The event is routed to the window under the pointer and bubbles to its ancestors the way every other input event does, so a control that ignores drops costs nothing and a container can answer for the whole of its content. A target commits to a drop by setting Gui.DragDropEvent.effect to one member of Gui.DragDropEvent.allowed; leaving it at None rejects the gesture and lets it bubble further.

Enter and Leave bracket the time the pointer spends over one window and are what a control showing a drop highlight turns on and off. Leave is also delivered when the user cancels the drag or drops it elsewhere, so a highlight is never left behind.

A target that shows the gesture repaints itself, the way it does for a mouse event: nothing is invalidated on its behalf, so a control that draws nothing costs nothing per pointer move.

struct Gui.FocusOrder #src

Keyboard traversal stops of one window tree, in the order the eye reads them.

The order is computed on demand instead of maintained, so a tree that has gained, lost, moved, hidden, or disabled a window since the last traversal needs no bookkeeping to stay correct.

Two rules produce it:

  • Depth first, so a subtree is traversed whole before its next sibling. Two forms side by side keep their own fields together instead of interleaving row by row.
  • Between siblings, the order their rectangles read in — rows from top to bottom, each row from left to right. The order a container creates its children in is not the order it places them: a docked command bar is created before the content that fills what is left over, and a stack that packs from the right hands back what it was given, reversed.

Every window whose policy is Gui.FocusPolicy.Tab is a stop, wherever it sits in the tree. A composite is therefore one stop because it says so once and leaves its inner windows on Gui.FocusPolicy.Click, and a tab control can be a stop for its bar while the page it shows keeps offering the stops of its own content. Hidden and disabled subtrees are left out entirely, and radio buttons sharing a group count as one stop, entered on the option that is checked.

struct FocusOrder

Fields

NameTypeDescription

Traversal stops of the collected tree, in reading order.

Collects the traversal stops of the whole tree wnd belongs to.

Returns the first stop, or null when the tree holds none.

Returns the position of the stop wnd belongs to, or -1 when it belongs to none.

Returns the last stop, or null when the tree holds none.

struct Gui.FormDlg #src

Modal dialog whose client area is a form the caller fills with typed fields.

Gui.FormDlg.create builds the surface, its centered form, and the standard buttons. Add the fields through the Gui.FormLayoutCtrl builders, arrange them once they are all present, then run the dialog. The height in Gui.FormDlgOptions is only what the surface starts at: Gui.FormDlg.doModal gives it the height the fields actually need.

let dlg = FormDlg.create(surface, options) let name = dlg.form.addTextField("FOLDER NAME", "New Folder") dlg.form.computeLayout() if dlg.doModal() == Dialog.BtnOk do createFolder(name.text())

struct Gui.FormLayoutCtrl #src

Arranges labeled fields from a compact row description instead of fixed coordinates.

The addTextField, addPasswordField, addChoiceField, and addOptionField builders create a control, append its row, and return the concrete control, so a caller never looks a field up by name. Add the optional trailing control of the row that was just appended with Gui.FormLayoutCtrl.addRowAction or Gui.FormLayoutCtrl.addRowChoice. Use Gui.FormLayoutCtrl.addField directly for a control the builders do not create.

The form owns the labels it creates and the layout of every row; the caller keeps the concrete control pointers.

let form = FormLayoutCtrl.create(parent) let path = form.addTextField("CONTAINER FILE", placeholder: "C:\\private.scrypt") let browse = form.addRowAction("Browse") let password = form.addPasswordField("PASSWORD") form.computeLayout()

struct Gui.HtmlView #src

Displays HTML as a laid-out document.

Gui.HtmlView.createText renders in-memory source, and Gui.HtmlView.createFile streams a file and follows local document links and stylesheets relative to its folder. Rendering stays offline: no script runs and remote references are reported through Gui.HtmlView.sigLinkActivated.

The document is parsed into a tree, styled through a real CSS cascade, and laid out into boxes, so a page keeps its columns, its tables, its inline styling, and the regions it scrolls on its own.

let document = HtmlView.createFile(parent, "manual.html") document.sigLinkActivated += func(view, url) { discard view Console.println(url) }

struct Gui.IconAtlas #src

Owns a vector icon document and the frames rasterized from it, at every size and density asked for.

The document is a uniform grid of 24-unit cells, one glyph per cell in row-major order. Rasterizing that grid is the expensive half of an icon set, and its pixels depend only on the document, the logical size, and the device scale — never on the renderer they end up in. An atlas therefore sits beside the document it owns and is shared by every Gui.IconSet built on it, so a process holding several themes rasterizes each sheet once instead of once per theme.

One atlas per document, for the lifetime of that document: the theme owns the one behind Gui.Theme.icon, and an application owns its own beside its icon source.

struct IconAtlas

Methods

NameDescription
setup

Parses source, an SVG document laid out as a uniform grid of 24-unit cells.

interface Gui.IPropertyEditor #src

A pluggable property editor. Register an implementing type with Properties.registerEditor (typically from a #init block); for each field the grid asks every registered editor whether it handles the field's type via canEdit, then builds the row via construct. This mirrors the image codec architecture (IImageDecoder / IImageEncoder): an interface + a type registry + per-use instantiation.

It is non-intrusive: the edited type is never touched. It lets ANY type (including primitives, enums, the built-in Color/vector types, or types you do not own) get a bespoke editor, registered from the outside. Because canEdit receives the type, one editor can claim a whole FAMILY of types (every enum, every type carrying a given attribute, a set of related structs), not just a single one — something a type-keyed map cannot express.

interface IPropertyEditor

NameDescription

Answers the label of a menu item every time the menu computes its layout.

An item built from a literal keeps the wording it was built with, because the string is copied into the item once. struct Gui.PdfView #src

Displays a PDF document with viewer-oriented zooming, panning, and page navigation.

The view opens a document through Gui.Pdf.Reader, so pages are decoded on demand and the displayed page stays decoded between paints. A page is vector art, and it is painted as such: every paint draws the decoded items straight through the widget's painter — the application renderer, not an offline rasterization — at the exact scale the page is shown at, zoom and monitor scale included. A zoom or pan step is therefore a transform change, not a raster: the page's images are uploaded to the renderer once per page, its typefaces are resolved once per page, and path tessellations are cached inside the decoded page itself.

The mouse wheel scrolls, Ctrl and the wheel zoom around the pointer, dragging pans, a double click toggles between fitted and actual size, and the arrow, page, Home and End keys turn pages. Embedded actions, scripts, and forms are never executed.

The page's text can be worked with: a drag over words selects them, a double click takes the word, Ctrl+C and the right-click menu copy the selection, and Gui.PdfView.findText searches the whole document and reveals what it finds.

let view = PdfView.create(parent) try view.open("document.pdf") view.setZoom(2.0)

type alias Gui.PropertyTextResolver #src

Turns a string declared by a property attribute into the text the grid shows.

The argument is the literal the attribute carries — #[Properties.Name("Thickness")] passes "Thickness" — and the result is what the reader sees. An attribute value is a compile-time constant, so this is what lets a declared wording act as a translation key. Answer null for a string the resolver does not own: the module that declared it answers next, and the declared wording is what remains when nobody does.

alias PropertyTextResolver = func(string)->#null string

struct Gui.Separator #src

Draws a plain rule between the docked block before it and the one after it.

The form carries the thickness and the color together, so a surface never repeats those measurements and every rule of an application agrees with the theme.

A rule is the last way to separate two groups, after a raised background and after spacing: one per group turns a window into a grid of boxes. Reach for Hairline where neither works, and for Accent once, across the top edge of an application surface.

struct Gui.Spinner #src

Reports that work is under way, without claiming to know how much is left.

The ring is drawn, never sampled from an atlas, so it is exact at any size and at any display density — a spinner is the one piece of theme art that is always in motion, which is exactly where a resampled bitmap shows. Use it for a wait with no measurable progress; a Gui.ProgressBar carrying Indeterminate says the same thing along a docked edge.

It animates while it is visible and costs nothing while it is not, so the caller only shows and hides it:

let busy = Spinner.create(view, {4, 4}) busy.hide()

Field details

defaultButton#

Window Enter stands for while no focused control claims it, or null for none.

This and Gui.Surface.cancelButton are what make a form answerable without the pointer: Enter runs the dominant action of the surface, Escape backs out of it. A focused button always answers Enter itself, so these two only speak for a keyboard that is somewhere else — in a field, in a list. Both are borrowed and never owned.

dpiScale#

Physical device pixels per logical unit on the monitor showing this surface. position is in physical screen pixels; the window tree, painting, and mouse surface coordinates are logical and map through this factor.

wnd_ShadowPixel.Color

Ink of the drop shadow. Its alpha is the darkening the shadow reaches where it meets the

Field details

focusRingOnAccent#

The same ring, on a control whose own fill is the accent.

The ring points in the accent, so drawn over a block of it there is nothing left to see — and the default action of a dialog, which is exactly the control the keyboard opens on, is such a block.

imageRect_Fg#

Tint a drawn image is multiplied by. White leaves the image alone, which is what an image wants: it carries its own colors and owes the theme nothing.

surfaceDisabled#

Tint a surface fades to while a modal box holds it. It multiplies the whole surface, so it is a dimming factor rather than a color.

wnd_Border#

Outline of a whole surface. It must be opaque: the same stroke runs past the caption ground and the body ground, so a translucent value takes both of them on and the outline visibly changes tone at the caption seam instead of reading as one line.

wnd_Shadow#

Ink of the drop shadow. Its alpha is the darkening the shadow reaches where it meets the body, not the alpha of any one ring: the shadow fades from nothing at the outer edge of the margin up to this value against the window.

struct Gui.ThemeImageRect #src

Describes a scalable region in the theme atlas.

struct ThemeImageRect

Fields

NameTypeDescription
cornerf32

Theme atlas region used for corner.

keepBordersRatiobool

Theme atlas region used for keep borders ratio.

radiusf32

Corner the tile draws, in logical pixels, for the parts that have to follow that shape

rectCore.Math.Rectangle

Theme atlas region used for rect.

Field details

radius#

Corner the tile draws, in logical pixels, for the parts that have to follow that shape without drawing it — the keyboard-focus ring is one. Zero means the tile has no single corner to follow: a square fill, a glyph, a blurred shadow.

A nine-slice places the corner region of the atlas one for one, so this is the radius the shape keeps at every control size, and it is never more than corner.

struct Gui.ThemeImageRects #src

Maps GUI parts to scalable regions in the theme atlas.

Several parts name the same atlas tile on purpose: a tile is a shape, and the shape of a round fill does not change because a toggle rather than a push button asks for it. What each part keeps of its own is the nine-slice corner and the radius it publishes, which is why two rects over one tile can still draw two different controls. theme/widgets.svg therefore holds each shape exactly once; an empty rect means the part draws nothing until a theme sheet points it somewhere.

Field details

chevron_Size#

Side of the box a chevron is drawn in — the drop-down of a field, the submenu marker of a menu entry, the disclosure of a tree or a property row, the sort order of a column, the arrow of a menu button. One decision for all of them, because they are one glyph (Gui.ThemeIcons.ChevronDown and its three siblings) and a reader reads them as one.

It is an indicator, not a control, so it sits at the smallest cell of the chart: the ink is five sixths of this box wide and half that tall.

surfaceWnd_ShadowSize#

Transparent margin the drop shadow is cast into. It has to hold the spread plus the offset, or the shadow is cut off by the edge of the window instead of fading out into it.

struct Gui.ThemePalette #src

The decisions a theme actually makes.

Gui.ThemeColors carries one value per painted part, which is what a widget needs and what a designer must never be asked to fill in: three hundred values written by hand are three hundred chances to answer for a control in one mode and forget it in the other, and that is exactly the defect a reader sees — a light theme keeping the blue hover of the palette it was derived from.

A palette is the short answer instead. Every semantic color is derived from these tokens by Gui.ThemeColors.apply, so a theme is complete by construction: there is no value it can leave unanswered, and the same rule produces the same relationship in every theme. A theme that wants one part different still says so afterwards, through a theme sheet.

The tokens are grouped by what they decide: where the reader is looking (grounds), what separates things (rules), what is written (ink), and which of a closed set of tones a thing belongs to.

Field details

captionGlow#

How far the caption band travels toward the signature block at the edge that carries the mark, from zero for a flat band.

It is a decision rather than a color, and nothing else predicts it: railed says how the active item is marked, not whether the chrome is tinted. A theme that follows the desktop keeps its caption flat; a theme that carries a brand lights the band from its own mark.

The band is the one surface of a window with no content to carry, which is what lets it carry the focus instead: an active window glows and an inactive one is flat, where two grounds ten levels apart reported nothing across a desktop.

The number is a mix, not a perceived amount, and the two do not track each other: a wash toward a color darker than the band is spent on luminance, which the eye reads at once, and a wash toward one as light as the band is spent on chroma, which costs three times as much mix to reach the same weight. A light theme therefore asks for a much larger number than a dark one for a band of the same strength, and a light theme that copied the dark number shipped a caption nobody could see.

railed#

Whether the theme marks the active item — a checked tool, the open menu, the selected row — with a rule in the signature, or by filling the item instead. It is a decision, not a color: a rail drawn in anything other than the signature says the item is active in a language the rest of the interface does not speak. Changing the signature therefore moves the rail with it, which is the whole reason this is not a color.

shadow#

Ink of a drop shadow. Its alpha is the darkening the shadow reaches where it meets the body it is cast by, not the alpha of any one ring.

veil#

Ink a translucent veil is made of: white over a dark ground, black over a light one. Every overlay of the theme is this color at one of three strengths, which is why a veil never has to be re-tuned per widget.

struct Gui.ThemeTone #src

One color of a theme, in the three roles a color is ever used in.

A theme never really has "a color". It has something to point with — a rail, a ring, a rule, a glyph, a word — something to fill with, and the ink that fill carries. Asking for the three together is what makes a tone impossible to half-answer, and what lets a palette hand the same color to all three when it can.

The three parting company is not an edge case, it is the identity: Voltage fills beautifully under ink and vanishes as a hairline on paper, so the light Swag theme points with a deepened Voltage and still fills with the brand one. Gui.ThemeColors.apply performs that deepening itself — see Gui.ThemeTone.mark.

Field details

children#

The child list is maintained by the window itself: attach through [setParent] and detach through [detachChild] so parent, surface, style, and layout state stay consistent.

focusDelegate#

Window the focus lands on when this one is given the focus, or null to take it.

A composite declares the policy on itself and delegates the focus to the inner window that actually handles the keys, so a caller holding the composite never has to know which part of it edits, scrolls, or draws a caret.

focusRingGround#

Fill the keyboard-focus ring will be drawn over, published the same way and for the same reason: the ring points in the accent, and a control filled with that accent would swallow it. A fully transparent value means the ring is not drawn over any known fill.

focusRingRadius#

Corner of the shape this window paints, which the keyboard-focus ring follows so the two never cross. A widget that draws a themed tile publishes it from that tile while painting — see Gui.ThemeImageRect.radius — because the tile a palette points a control at is the only thing that knows whether the control is a pill or a square this frame.

Left at zero the ring keeps the soft corner of Gui.ThemeMetrics.focusRing_Radius, which is what a control with no shape of its own — a check box and its label, a slider, a tab — should be marked with.

Field details

paragraphAlignment#

Horizontal alignment of body paragraphs.

Justify spreads the spaces of every wrapped line so both edges of the column are flush. A line the author ended, and the last line of a paragraph, keep their natural width; a line whose spaces would have to stretch past twice the line height is left ragged rather than pulled apart. Headings, lists, quotes, tables and code are never justified.

Returns the document style that follows the active GUI theme.

struct ToolTip.State #src

The live tool tip of one application.

Gui.Application owns one, for the same reason it owns the focus and the drag: a tip is one pointer's state over one window tree. Held per process instead, two applications in a process would share a single tip, and one left open at the end of a test would reach the next test and destroy a window whose surface has already gone.

enum Gui.EditBoxFlags #src

Optional behaviour modifiers for the EditBox.

#[Swag.EnumFlags] enum EditBoxFlags

Cases

NameDescription
AcceptFileDrop

Makes a file dragged from the desktop replace the content with its path.

ClearButton

Shows a clear button while content is non-empty.

None

Uses editable left-aligned text without a clear button.

ReadOnly

Prevents edits while preserving focus and selection.

ReleaseFocusOnEnterOrEscape

Makes the box an edit of its own that Enter and Escape end.

RightAligned

Aligns text to the trailing edge.

Case details

AcceptFileDrop#

Makes a file dragged from the desktop replace the content with its path.

This is what a field naming a document is for: one file dropped anywhere on the box fills it, exactly as picking that file from a browse dialog would, and the box emits its usual change notification. A drag carrying several files is refused, because a single field has nothing to say about the others. Without this flag a box still takes dropped text, which is what every text field on the desktop does.

ReleaseFocusOnEnterOrEscape#

Makes the box an edit of its own that Enter and Escape end.

Enter submits it, Escape puts back the text the box held when it took the focus, and both release the focus and keep the key. This is for a box that stands for a passing task — renaming an item in place, filtering a list — and never for a field of a form, whose Enter belongs to the dialog's default action and whose Escape dismisses the dialog.

enum Gui.FocusPolicy #src

Selects how a window takes part in keyboard focus.

One policy answers both questions a window has about the focus: whether a pointer press gives it the focus, and what the keyboard traversal of Gui.FocusOrder does when it reaches it.

A composite stands in the traversal once, as one control, however many windows it is built from: it declares Tab on itself, points Gui.Wnd.focusDelegate at the window that reads the keys, and declares Inner on that window so nothing it builds below shows up as a second stop beside it.

enum FocusPolicy

Cases

NameDescription
Click

Takes the focus when pressed, without being a stop; the traversal walks through.

Inner

Takes the focus when pressed, and hides itself and its children from the traversal.

None

Never takes the keyboard focus; the traversal walks through to the children.

Tab

Takes the focus when pressed, and is one stop of the traversal.

const Gui.MarkGlyphContrast #src

How much contrast the glyph of a mark owes a caption band before the band is allowed to show it without its tile. Three is where a shape stops being separated from what it is drawn over.

const Gui.MarkInk #src

The two colors every Swag product mark is cut from, one glyph over one ground.

A drawn caption keys the ground out with them, so it needs no second copy of the icon, and it compares the glyph against its own band to decide whether keying it out is legible at all. They are the identity colors and nothing else: a mark that drifts from them stops being one.

Replaces one visible page with another using a covered cross-fade and horizontal arrival.

func Application.appIconAt #src

Returns the application mark at size logical pixels, cut to sit on ground, or an invalid icon when the application declares none.

The mark ships flattened — one glyph over one ink tile — because that is what a taskbar, a file list and an installer need. A drawn caption has a ground of its own, so on a dark band the tile is keyed out and the glyph floats free, where the tile would have read as a black square around it.

On a light band it cannot be, and this is the whole reason ground is asked for: the glyph is Voltage, and Voltage on paper is a mark nobody sees. The tile stays there, and the window carries the identity the way the chart says a light surface has to — as a block of brand rather than as a hairline of it. Below the threshold a keyed-out mark simply disappeared from the title bar of every application in the light theme.

Both cuts are uploaded once, on the first call, so this can be asked for from inside a paint without costing anything after the first frame.

mtd appIconAt(size: f32, ground: Pixel.Color)->Icon

Runs a nested event loop for surface and returns the identifier passed to exitModal.

Other enabled surfaces are disabled for the duration of the loop and restored to their previous state afterwards. The modal surface is destroyed when the loop ends.

restoreTo is the surface the keyboard belongs to once the box is gone — the one that raised it. It is asked for its own focus rather than being handed a position captured here, because a box that opens ready for the keyboard has already moved it onto itself by the time this runs: what was read here was a rank inside the box, applied to the ring of the form underneath it. See Surface.focusWnd.

func Application.registerFrameEvent #src

Asks for Gui.IWnd.onFrameEvent on target at the start of every rendered frame.

A surface view is sent one FrameEvent before the loop starts, carrying firstFrame; that is a startup hook. This is the per-frame half, and it is how a window defers work to the next frame — a rebuild asked for from inside a change notification, where rebuilding on the spot would destroy the control that is reporting.

Registration was internal and had no caller, so sendFrameEvents walked an empty array for the whole run and every deferral written against it silently never happened.

Register once and unregister before the window goes; Application.destroyWnd also drops a destroyed window from the list, so a normal teardown needs nothing.

mtd registerFrameEvent(target: *Wnd)

Scheduling a target window for destruction retires its timers, so a window that still names one from its own cleanup lands here on a timer this application no longer owns. The registry is what answers that: once a retirement has been flushed the timer is released, and reading its own fields to recognize the duplicate request would read freed memory.

func Application.setLanguage #src

Applies the language tag to every registered string table and refreshes every surface.

Gui.ReferenceLanguage restores the built-in reference strings. Any other tag resets the tables to their reference values, then applies the lang/<tag>/<file>.tweak resource of each registered table; a table without a file for that tag keeps its reference strings. Fails when the tag is not registered through Gui.registerLanguage or has no language file for any registered table, so a mistyped tag cannot silently present itself as applied. Menus and command-driven controls pick the new strings up on their next update; text set once at construction keeps its wording until the window is created again, so a window that must follow the switch listens for the Gui.NotifyEvent.Kind.LanguageChanged notification.

mtd setLanguage(tag: string) fail

func Dialog.doModal #src

Runs the dialog modally and returns the accepted button identifier.

The box opens ready for the keyboard: the focus goes where Gui.Dialog.keyboardEntry says, unless the caller already placed it, so a dialog can be answered and dismissed without the pointer.

The ring showing where the keys will go is turned on with the box rather than by the first Tab. A modal is a question, and the reader has to be told what pressing Enter now decides.

mtd doModal()->WndId
func Dialog.keyboardEntry #src

Returns the control the box opens the keyboard on, or null to take the reading order.

A box with something to fill in opens on that, and its default action still answers Enter, because a field hands the key on rather than consuming it. Anything the reader would act on with a key is passed over, whatever it is and wherever it reads: a push button presses, a check box or a toggle flips a preference, a radio button selects. Those all say so with Gui.WndFlags.ActivatesOnKey, so nothing here has to know one kind of button from another.

A box made only of them is a question, and it opens on the action it names as its default rather than on whichever control reads first — which is how a confirmation defaulting to No would have answered Yes, and how one carrying a Do not ask again option opened on the option instead of on the question. Tab still reaches everything; this is only where the keyboard starts.

mtd keyboardEntry()->#null *Wnd

func FocusOrder.nextInGroup #src

Returns the stop before or after from inside its own group, wrapping around that group.

A group is the stops that share one parent: the buttons of a command bar, the options of a panel, the fields a form places on one line. It is what the arrow keys walk, the way a dialog box walks the controls of one group and leaves Tab to cross the whole box — so Left and Right on an action bar choose between the actions instead of wandering into the content above them.

A stop alone in its group has no group to walk, and answering nothing would make the arrows read as broken on exactly the surfaces that place one control per row. It falls back to the full ring, which is Gui.FocusOrder.next.

mtd const nextInGroup(from: #null *Wnd, forward = true)->#null *Wnd

func Gui.applyLanguage #src

Applies the language tag to every registered string table.

Gui.ReferenceLanguage restores the declared reference strings. Any other tag first resets each table, then decodes its lang/<tag>/<file>.tweak resource from resources; a table without a file for that tag keeps its reference strings.

Fails without touching any table when the tag is not registered through Gui.registerLanguage, or when no registered table has a file for it, so a mistyped tag cannot present itself as applied; a malformed file fails mid-way with the earlier tables already switched.

resources is remembered while the tag stays active, so a table registered later is translated from the same bundle instead of waiting for the next switch. Prefer Application.setLanguage, which also notifies every surface. GUI thread only.

func applyLanguage(resources: const *Resources.Bundle, tag: string) fail

A modifier naming an effect the source refuses falls back the same way, so the returned value is always a member of allowed or None.

func Gui.registerLanguage #src

Registers a language the interface can present.

tag is a short language tag such as "fr", and nativeName is the name of the language written in that language, because a picker lists it beside the others rather than inside a translated sentence. Registering a tag again replaces its name. Gui.ReferenceLanguage is always registered and always comes first. A module or an application registers its own tag next to the resources that carry it. GUI thread only.

func registerLanguage(tag, nativeName: string)
func Gui.registerStrings #src

Registers a string table so language switches retarget it.

table is borrowed for the whole program: a global of the module or the application that owns it, or of a shared library that is never unloaded, since a registration cannot be withdrawn. file names the per-language resource, resolved as lang/<tag>/<file>.tweak. Registering the same table again is a no-op.

The table is translated on the spot when a language is already active, so a table that arrives with a library loaded on demand shows the language already on screen rather than waiting for the next switch. Add its resource to the bundle first. GUI thread only.

func(T) registerStrings(table: *T, file: string)

Registers a string table through its reflected type; prefer the typed overload.

func ImageView.exchangeImage #src

Displays image by exchanging pixel storage with the view instead of copying it.

A source that produces a new picture many times a second — a decoded video stream, a camera, a live render — otherwise pays a full copy of every picture on the very thread that has to present it, and at high resolutions that copy is the same order of magnitude as the upload it feeds. Here the view takes the pixels of image and leaves its own in their place, so the caller keeps a buffer of exactly the right shape to produce the next picture into and nothing is copied.

image must carry the geometry and pixel format the view is already showing. Anything else behaves like Gui.ImageView.setImage, which copies and refits.

try decoder.decodeFrameInto(&frame, index) view.exchangeImage(&frame) // `frame` now owns the picture that just left the screen
mtd exchangeImage(image: *Image)

func ImageView.replaceImage #src

Replaces the image with another rendering of the same content, keeping the view.

A viewer whose content is scalable — a document page, a drawing — does not zoom by magnifying pixels: it rasterizes again at the resolution it is now being shown at, so the result stays as sharp as the display allows. What it must not do is lose the reader's place while doing so. scaleRatio is how much larger the new image is than the one it replaces, which is what lets the zoom follow the content instead of the pixel count and leaves the visible region exactly where it was.

let sharper = renderPage(pageIndex, newScale) view.replaceImage(sharper, newScale / oldScale)
mtd replaceImage(image: Image, scaleRatio: f32)

mtd updateImage(image: const *Image)
func ImageView.updateVideoFrame #src

Displays a planar 4:2:0 picture, which the renderer converts while it draws.

This is what a video stream should reach the screen through. Converting a picture to packed RGB costs more processor time at high resolutions than decoding it did, and none of it is needed: the renderer holds the planes the decoder produced and converts them where it samples. The view never owns the picture, so view is borrowed for the call alone.

try reader.decodeFramePlanesInto(&picture, index) view.updateVideoFrame(picture.view())
mtd updateVideoFrame(view: const *Yuv420View)

func IPropertyEditor.construct #src

Build the editor row(s) for value (the field at data) under parent and return the created item — exactly like the built-in construct* methods. The recipe: call list.addItem(value, data, parent), create the editor widget(s) under item.line, wire their change callbacks to list.commitItemChange(item), and add an item.sigRefresh handler that pushes the current value back into the widget(s). See values/color.swg and values/vector.swg.

An editor is a stateless singleton: it is invoked on a null instance (like canEdit), so me carries no per-field state — read any per-field configuration from value (its attributes), and wire data/item/list into the widget callbacks.

func IWnd.measureContent #src

Returns the size this window's own content needs, or zero on an axis it cannot answer.

A window that draws text, an icon, or items answers with what showing them whole costs, so a caption never has to be measured by hand at the call site. available is the space the container can offer, which is what a window whose height follows its width — wrapped text — answers against; a zero component means the container has no constraint to give on that axis.

This is a query, not a routed event: it is asked of one window and never bubbles. Gui.Wnd.measure uses the answer only on an axis the author left unsized, so an explicit size always wins.

mtd measureContent(available: Math.Point)->Math.Point

Says where a drop released at surfacePos would land.

The outer quarter of a row reads as the gap next to it and the middle half reads as the row itself, which is the convention a file manager trains every reader on. A position past the last row answers the gap after it, so a list is appended to by aiming at its empty part, and an empty list answers Before on row zero.

This is only the geometry. What a drop means is the window's decision, so a list that inserts and a list that drops onto a row both call this and then keep the answer they want.

mtd dropMarkAt(surfacePos: Math.Point)->{ index: u32, mark: ListDropMark }

func Properties.setTextResolver #src

Installs the resolver every string a property attribute declares passes through.

Every label, description, category segment, heading, note, unit, and enumeration entry the grid generates from reflection is resolved through resolver, so an application that translates its interface makes #[Properties.Name("Thickness")] a key rather than a final wording. One resolver serves every grid in the process, and the strings this module declares itself are resolved after it, so an application only answers for its own. Pass null to show the declared strings again.

Install it before building a grid — a row already built keeps the text it was created with — and rebuild the grids that must follow a language switch. GUI thread only.

Properties.setTextResolver(func(key: string)->#null string { switch key { case "Thickness": return appStrings().prop_Thickness } return null })

func PushButton.fitWidthToLabel #src

Pins the button width to its label instead of leaving it to the layout pass.

A button created without a width already follows its caption, so this is for a button that must carry a settled width right away — one placed by hand, or one that has to agree with a sibling before any container measures it. minWidth keeps a floor under very short captions. Call it again after changing the name, the icon, or the emphasis.

mtd fitWidthToLabel(minWidth: f32 = 0)
func PushButton.paintedForm #src

Returns the emphasis the button is drawn with, which is not always the one it was given.

A surface that names a dominant action draws it filled, and the reader takes that fill to mean "this is what Enter runs". A focused button runs Enter itself, so once the keyboard stands on another action the fill has to be there and not on the one the box was built around — otherwise the box shows two answers to the same question, and the wrong one is the loud one. It goes back to the named action as soon as the keyboard leaves the bar.

Only the two plain emphases take part. A flat button belongs to a tool bar, and a filled one — strong or alternate — carries its own tone through every state; none of them stands for the answer to a box.

mtd paintedForm()->PushButtonForm

func RadioButton.selectSibling #src

Selects the next or previous option of this button's group, and reports whether one was found.

The order is the order the options were created in and it wraps, so the arrows stay inside the group however long they are held: a group that let the last option pass the key on would hand the keyboard to whatever stands beside it, which is what Tab is for. An ungrouped button has nothing to move to. The selected option takes the keyboard with it, so the ring keeps standing on the option that is checked.

mtd selectSibling(forward: bool)->bool

func State.show #src

Shows str near surfacePos, after delay, for owner.

str is Pixel.RichString markup, so a tip is not limited to one flat sentence: it can set bold, italic and underline, reach the three palette colors with <pN>, and carry <url> spans the reader can click. A tip holding a link stays while the pointer is over it and reports the activation through Gui.ToolTip.State.sigLinkActivated; one holding none is passive and goes as soon as the pointer reaches it.

The tip is exactly as large as the text it holds. Past Gui.ThemeMetrics.toolTip_MaxWidth it wraps rather than grow, past Gui.ThemeMetrics.toolTip_MaxHeight it ends its last line with an ellipsis rather than grow, and it never scrolls — so a caller can hand it any length knowing the reader is shown a box, not a viewport onto something longer. Keep a tip to what fits: text the height cap truncates is text nobody reads.

func Theme.applySheet #src

Applies a theme sheet to this theme.

A sheet is a tweak text with up to four folders whose keys are the reflected field names of Gui.ThemePalette, Gui.ThemeColors, Gui.ThemeMetrics and Gui.ThemeImageRects. An omitted key keeps its current value, so a sheet only describes what it changes, and $name copies another key of the same folder:

/ThemePalette ground 0xFF161310 text 0xFFEDE4D4 accent 0xFFD79921 /ThemeColors btnPush_Bk 0xFF202026 /ThemeMetrics btnPush_Height 32 /ThemeImageRects btnPush_Normal {{1 29 27 27} 0} btnPush_Hot $btnPush_Normal

A whole theme is written in the first folder: naming any palette token re-derives every color from the tokens, so a sheet of thirty lines answers for the three hundred parts of the interface and cannot leave one of them behind. The other folders are for the parts a theme wants different from what its own tokens derive, and they are read after the derivation whatever order they appear in.

An unknown key or a malformed value fails with Core.Errors.SyntaxError carrying the line number; the theme keeps the values already applied before the error. Call Gui.Application.notifyThemeChanged afterwards when the theme is already on screen.

mtd applySheet(sheet: string) fail

func Theme.drawFocusRing #src

Draws the ring that says the keyboard focus is on rect.

Call it at the end of the paint of a control that has nothing else to show for the focus — a button, a check box, a picker. A field with a caret and a list with a selected row already say it, and a second mark on them would only be noise.

The ring is a rule inside the control, inset by Gui.ThemeMetrics.focusRing_Inset so it never merges with the control's own border. Draw it only while Gui.Wnd.showsFocusRing holds, so a control pressed with the pointer stays unmarked.

corner is the corner of the control, which the ring follows: stepped in by the inset it stays concentric with the outline it sits inside, and a pill keeps its ends round instead of carrying a box. A control with no shape of its own — a check box and its label, a slider, a tab — passes zero and gets Gui.ThemeMetrics.focusRing_Radius, which is the softest corner the ring ever takes.

ground is the fill the ring will be drawn over, which a control publishes so the ring can be read on it: the accent is what the theme points with, but a control filled with that same accent — the default action of a dialog, a switched-on toggle, a picked tool — would swallow it. Left at zero the ring keeps the accent. See Gui.ThemeColors.focusRingOnAccent.

mtd drawFocusRing(painter: *Painter, rect: Math.Rectangle, corner = 0'f32, ground: Color = {})

func Theme.ensureAtlasScale #src

Keeps the widgets atlas texture at least as sharp as scale device pixels per authored texel.

The vector theme document is the source of truth; the atlas texture is only its cached rasterization, rebuilt here so themed drawing stays one textured blit at native resolution. The scale is rounded up to a whole number so the nine-slice source cuts of ThemeImageRects stay on texel boundaries: on a fractional grid every tile border would sample its neighbor. The atlas only sharpens; a request at or below the current scale returns immediately, so a surface moving to a coarser monitor keeps the sharp atlas, which minifies cleanly.

mtd ensureAtlasScale(renderer: IRenderer, scale: f32)

func ThemeColors.swagDarkPalette #src

The dark Swag palette: Voltage and Arc over Ink.

The signature is the mark's own yellow, and nothing here washes a row with it: Voltage is a color to point with, never a color to read on. That is exactly what the second tone is for — an electric blue that can be a block, a row, a link and a mode without ever being mistaken for the one thing to do. The signature stays spent on marks, rails and the one filled action.

func swagDarkPalette()->ThemePalette
func ThemeColors.swagLightPalette #src

The light Swag palette: Voltage and Arc over Paper.

It is the dark palette read the other way up, not a second identity, and it says so by declaring the same two tones with the same two numbers. What the mode changes is only what a tone may point with: a block survives the trip and a hairline does not, so the theme deepens each mark until it separates from the page and fills with the brand color untouched. Written that way, a light Swag surface carries the same yellow block, the same blue rows and the same family of hues as a dark one.

The previous light theme pointed in ink instead of deepening, and that one decision is what made it read as a black-and-white theme with a yellow button rather than as the same theme on paper.

Its greys carry the violet cast of the dark palette's, so the two are one family. Warm paper under cool ink was the other half of the inelegance: no surface here is neutral, and every one of them was leaning the wrong way.

func swagLightPalette()->ThemePalette

func Wnd.setInitialFocus #src

Gives the keyboard focus to the first traversal stop of this window's tree.

Call it once a surface is fully built, so it opens ready for the keyboard: a form the user can start typing into, a dialog that answers Tab from its first field. A focus that already stands somewhere inside this tree is left where it is — the caller placed it on purpose — and a tree with no stop at all keeps none.

preferred is the stop to open on when the reading order is not what the surface means by "start here": a box whose answer is a default action opens on that action, so the first Enter presses what the box says it will and not what happens to read first. It is ignored when it is not a stop of this tree.

mtd setInitialFocus(preferred: #null *Wnd = null)

See Gui.ApplicationOptions.showFocusRings.

mtd showsFocusRing()->bool
func Wnd.startDrag #src

Carries data to whatever the pointer is released on, and returns what was done with it.

This runs the gesture: it does not return until the user drops or gives up, because the desktop owns the pointer for the whole of it. The payload is borrowed and has to outlive the call, which a local of the calling frame does by construction. allowed is what the target may choose from; the answer is the single effect it settled on, or None when the drag was cancelled or refused.

picture is what the desktop draws under the pointer for the length of the gesture, and defaults to the picture the payload already carries. A drag with nothing under the cursor but an arrow reads as a lesser gesture than the same drag out of a file manager, so a source that carries no image of its own is worth handing one.

One thing follows from the desktop running the loop: the button that started the drag comes back up inside it, so a control tracking a press has to forget it here rather than waiting for a release event that has already been consumed. The application keeps drawing, from the feedback callback the same loop makes.

Answers None immediately with no native window, which is what a headless test gets.

mtd startDrag(data: *DragData, allowed = DropEffect.Copy, picture: #null const *Pixel.Image = null)->DropEffect
